31676-heathen-master-filcsik:
Kálmán Mikszáth's short story Heathen Master Filcsik comes into English from the Magyar in a translation by William N. Loew, printed at Cleveland at the Clerk's Private Press in 1910. An introductory note explains that Loew placed the manuscript at the publisher's disposal. It adds that the tale is one of the shorter stories of a living Hungarian writer.

The note adds that Magyar literature is a gold mine for translators, though few have explored it. Most first-class Hungarian authors besides the novelist Maurus Jókai remain unknown to the average American reader. Filcsik's tale is offered as a sample of that untranslated wealth.
55334-the-philosophy-of-fine-art-volume-:
The Philosophy of Fine Art, volume one of four, by G W F Hegel, in English by F P B Osmaston, was printed in London by G Bell and Sons in 1920. Osmaston had written The Art and Genius of Tintoret. The set gives Hegel Aesthetik in full English dress.

In his preface Osmaston says the work is the first complete English version of the three volumes on this subject in the Berlin collected edition of 1835. He knows four partial English versions and one French. He names Bryant version of part two, Kedney short study, Hastie work on Michelet, and Bosanquet full version of the first opening with notes. The French version, he holds, is in large part a free summary. Thought fans get the great German system of art in full.
55445-the-philosophy-of-fine-art-volume-:
The Philosophy of Fine Art, volume two of four, is Hegel's lectures on art in a translation by Osmaston. The volume covers the second great part of the work, on the symbolic type of art. A long contents list breaks the argument into fine steps. Notes by the translator run with the text.

The opening treats the symbol itself, as more than a mere sign. A symbol presents the very quality it stands for, yet stays open to doubt and double sense. The text asks how far symbolism deserves rank as a form of art. Chapters then pass through types of symbolism in order. The religion of Zoroaster shows meaning and form still one. Hindu thought shows symbolism grown wild and measureless. The final aim of symbolic art, Hegel argues, is classical art, where it dissolves.
55623-the-philosophy-of-fine-art-volume-:
The Philosophy of Fine Art, by Hegel, in Osmaston's English translation, reaches its third volume here. Bell issued it at London in 1920. Volume three holds the third part of the work, the system of the particular arts. Hegel sorts the arts by how spirit takes shape in matter that the senses can grasp.

The first subsection treats architecture, the most material of the arts. It begins with buildings raised to unite peoples, and works set between building and sculpture. Obelisks of Egypt, temple enclosures, and labyrinths serve as examples. Then comes the passage to self standing architecture in its own right. Later pages reach the Gothic church, with its piers, choir, transept, nave, and aisles. Hegel's lectures on art shaped how the West thinks about beauty. This volume shows his system at its most detailed.
55731-the-philosophy-of-fine-art-volume-:
The Philosophy of Fine Art, volume four, by G W F Hegel, turned into English by F P B Osmaston, came out in London in 1920. Osmaston had written on the art and genius of Tintoret. This volume ends a long course on the fine arts, and gives its whole bulk to poetry.

Hegel treats poetry as the last of the romantic arts. He asks what makes a poem a work of art, not mere prose in verse dress. A poem must hold one life in its parts, he holds, as a chord holds its notes. Past tales and fine speech come close to poetry, yet serve set ends. Free poetry serves no such end, and stands round and whole in itself. A last part treats the urge that drives the poet. Students get Hegel at his most dense and rich.
67082-nick-carter-stories-no-11-november:
Street and Smith issued Nick Carter Stories weekly from 79 Seventh Avenue, New York. Number 11 bears the date November 23, 1912. Five cents bought a number, and post terms ran from sixty-five cents for three months.

The head of this number is all business paper: the ownership statement the law of August 24, 1912, forced on magazines. Blackwell edits at 32 West 75th Street. The Smith brothers own the whole, and no bondholder holds a share, the sworn page says. Such dry print is itself a relic of the great story papers at their peak. Carter, the king of detectives, fought a fresh foe each week for a nation of boys.
67426-bantu-beliefs-and-magic-with-parti:
Bantu Beliefs and Magic is a work of anthropology by Hobley, late senior provincial commissioner in Kenya Colony, published by Witherby of London in 1922. Sir James Frazer wrote the introduction. Hobley treats the Kikuyu and Kamba peoples in particular, and adds reflections on East Africa after the war. The first part, Natural Religion, covers spirit beliefs and sacrifice.

Sacred stones, village shrines, firstfruits, and the harvest and planting ceremonies follow. Circumcision, death, and burial ceremonies come next, then the curse in its forms and purification. The second part, Magic, treats the guild of smiths, the evil eye, and Kikuyu magicians. A third part ranges wider: the working of councils, laws of compensation for murder, ceremonial oaths, war and peace, legends, and dances. Hobley wrote from years of colonial service among the peoples he describes.
74474-first-lessons-in-batik:
Gertrude Clayton Lewis, an art teacher at a Chicago high school, wrote this handbook on batik and tie-dyeing, printed under copyright in 1921. Batik, the wax and dye craft of Java, was new and fashionable in America. Lewis gives detailed directions for doing the work under American conditions, with set problems to try.

She promises gowns, scarfs, table covers, bags, and curtains that carry the maker's own touch. Since the beauty of the work rests on personal taste, she argues, it cannot easily be mass produced, and good pieces sell well. The book aims at artists, teachers, and craft workers, and at art classes in schools and colleges. A batik wall hanging from the Art Institute of Chicago fronts the lessons.
britannica-1911-abel-niels-henrik:
Niels Henrik Abel receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abel, a Norwegian mathematician born at Findöe in 1802, proved his genius at Christiania's cathedral school by solving Holmboë's problems. A poor minister's son, he reached the university on a small state pension.

His proof that the quintic equation cannot be solved by radicals came first, in 1824. Travel in 1825 brought him to Crelle in Berlin and to Paris, where fame lagged and funds failed. Elliptic, hyperelliptic, and the new Abelian functions bear his mark. Crelle won him a Berlin post in 1829; the offer reached Norway after his death near Arendal. Legendre's praise heads the close: what a head that young Norwegian had.
britannica-1911-acharius-erik:
Erik Acharius (1757-1819) was a Swedish botanist who entered Upsala University in 1773 as a pupil of Linnaeus, the great classifier of plants. He took his medical degree at Lund in 1782 and became professor of botany at Wadstena Academy in 1801. The short Britannica biography gives a life narrowed to one devoted subject.

Lichens claimed all his work. Every publication Acharius produced dealt with that class of plants, the crusty growths formed by fungi and algae living together. His Lichenographia Universalis, published at Gottingen in 1804, is named as the most important of them. He died at Wadstena in 1819, having given lichen study its early system.
britannica-1911-ahmed-vefik:
Ahmed Vefik Pasha, Turkish statesman and man of letters of 1819 to 1891, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Stambul, he was the son of Rouheddin Effendi, a fine French scholar who served on Reshid Pasha's mission to Paris. Reshid took the boy along and schooled him there for about five years. Ahmed returned to a post in the foreign ministry's translation bureau.

In his spare hours he translated Moliere's plays into Turkish and compiled dictionaries and school manuals to spread French learning. He launched the Salnameh, the Ottoman official annual, in 1847, and served as imperial commissioner in the Danubian principalities. Briefly prime minister in 1878, he later governed Brusa for nearly four years. There he drained marshes, brought mountain water, built roads, suppressed brigandage, and multiplied schools.
britannica-1911-bilejik:
Bilejik, known in Byzantine times as Belocome, is a town in Asia Minor. It is the chief town of the Ertoghrul sanjak in the Brusa vilayet. The town stands on a hill at 1,900 feet above the sea. Its railway station, on the Ismid to Angora line, lies 22 miles away. The 1911 Britannica entry gives a population of 10,500. Of those people, 7,200 are listed as Moslems and 3,300 as Christians.

Silk is the town's key industry, the entry says. Several silk-spinning factories work there, making Bilejik an important centre of that trade. The entry runs to just three short sentences in total. It gives no history beyond the old Byzantine name. No buildings, markets, or leaders are named. The hill site, the mixed population, and the silk mills are the whole picture the text supports.
britannica-1911-birejik:
Birejik is a town of north-west Mesopotamia, in the Aleppo vilayet. It stands 1,170 feet up, on a limestone cliff 400 feet high. Below it runs the left bank of the Euphrates river. Its population is about 10,000, three-quarters of them Moslem. The town guards one of the Euphrates' most important crossings. A ferry now works the road from Aleppo toward Urfa, Diarbekr, and Mosul. In ancient times a bridge of boats crossed at the spot.

The place matches Apamea, which faced Zeugma across the river, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Its castle, Kala Beda, commanded the bridge and now lies much ruined. An older name, Birtha, came back under Roman rule and survives today. The emperor Julian rested there on his march in AD 363. The ferry ranked second only to Thapsacus for crossings south. A cruel massacre of Armenians there in 1895 closes the entry.
britannica-1911-conscience-hendrik:
Hendrik Conscience is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a Flemish writer who lived from 1812 to 1883. He was born at Antwerp in December 1812. His signed name was Hendrik, though baptized Henri. His father was a Frenchman who had served at sea. His father later kept ships gear at Antwerp port. His mother was a Fleming of that city.

When French rule ended the father stayed in Antwerp. He took to buying and breaking up worn out ships. The boy grew up in an old shop of sea stores. Unsold books were kept in that shop as well. Old tales among them fired the child love of story. His mother died in the year 1820. Grim home life with his father marks the tale. A love of reading grew in him all day long.
britannica-1911-dahlgren-karl-fredrik:
Karl Fredrik Dahlgren, a Swedish poet who lived from 1791 to 1844, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Stensbruk in Ostergotland in June 1791. Swedish writers of his day split into two camps, the Goths and the Phosphorists. Dahlgren made himself vital to the Phosphorists by his sharp pen.

He had a true gift for humour, shown in a mock heroic poem that mocked a rival scholar. In 1825 he published a satire called The Tower of Babel and a comedy, and in 1828 two volumes of poems. From 1819 his odes sought to match the lyric genius of Bellman, whom he studied and followed. He edited a critical journal, The Comet, from 1825 to 1827. The entry calls him one of the best humorous writers Sweden has produced.
britannica-1911-goltzius-hendrik:
Hendrik Goltzius, a Dutch painter and engraver, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in fifteen fifty eight in the duchy of Julich, he first studied painting on glass under his father. He was then taught the engraver's tool by a Dutch engraver. He soon passed his teacher in skill.

He was also employed to engrave a set of prints on the tale of Lucretia. At twenty one he wed a widow whose money let him set up his own business at Haarlem. His home life was unhappy, the entry notes. The text follows his work and the fame his prints brought him across Europe.
britannica-1911-haik: Haik is a piece of cloth worn by Arabs, Moors, and other Muslim peoples. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes the name from an Arabic word for weaving. The cloth is most often coarse hand woven wool, striped or plain. It runs about six yards long and two yards broad. Both men and women wear it as an outer wrap. For the poor it is often the only garment. Women draw it to cover the head and face before men, and brides use a thin silk form as a veil.
britannica-1911-hasselquist-frederik:
Hasselquist, Frederik, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a Swedish traveller. Born at Tornevalla on the 3rd of January 1722, he read at Upsala. There he studied under the great naturalist Linnaeus as a pupil. Linnaeus often rued how little was known of Palestine's plants and beasts.

That lack drove Hasselquist to plan a trip to that land. Funds were raised by subscription to pay for the trip. He reached Smyrna late in 1749 and toured Asia Minor and Egypt. Cyprus and Palestine were also on his route of travel. He made large collections of plants and beasts as he went. Weak health gave way, and he died near Smyrna in 1752. Linnaeus brought out his trip notes five years after his death.
britannica-1911-laurvik:
Laurvik, also spelled Larvik or Laurvig, is a seaport of Norway. It lies in the county of Jarlsberg and Laurvik, at the head of a short fjord near the mouth of the Laagen river. It is ninety-eight miles south-west of Christiania by the Skien railway. The town had 10,664 people in 1900. Its port has water eighteen to twenty-four feet deep beside the quays.

Trades in Laurvik include saw and planing mills, shipbuilding, and glass works. Works there make wood pulp, barrels, and potato flour. The town ships out timber, ice, wood pulp, and granite, chiefly to Great Britain. It brings in coal and salt from the same land. Four miles south lies Fredriksvaern, once a base of the Norwegian fleet. Laurviks Bad is a prized spa with mineral and sulphur springs and mud baths.
britannica-1911-ling-per-henrik:
Swedish medical gymnastic practitioner Per Henrik Ling, born at Ljunga in seventeen seventy six, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a minister. He studied divinity and took his degree in seventeen ninety seven. He then went abroad for some years.

He taught modern languages at Copenhagen, then travelled in Germany, France, and England. Lack of money harmed his health, and he suffered much from joint pain. Yet he gained great skill in gymnastics and fencing. Back in Sweden he taught those arts at Lund. Daily exercise restored his own health in full. He then studied the body and medicine, and built a system of gymnastics in four branches. In eighteen thirteen a royal institute for training teachers opened in Stockholm, with him as its head.
britannica-1911-reusch-hans-henrik:
Hans Henrik Reusch, born at Bergen in 1852, is profiled in a short life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Norwegian geologist who trained at Christiania, Leipzig, and Heidelberg. He joined the Geological Survey of Norway in 1875. He rose to lead that survey as its director in 1888.

The entry sums up his work on the old rocks of Norway. He found Silurian fossils in rocks near Bergen that heat and force had much changed. He also pointed to an old bed of boulders by the Varanger Fiord as proof of ice at work in a far past age. His books on the rocks of north Norway are named at the close.
britannica-1911-steffens-henrik:
Henrik Steffens (1773–1845) was a German philosopher, scientist, and poet of Norwegian stock, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his studies. He was born on the second of May 1773 at Stavanger. He died in Berlin on the thirteenth of February 1845. At fourteen he went with his parents to Copenhagen.

At Copenhagen Steffens studied theology and natural science side by side. In 1796 he lectured at Kiel, and a year later went to Jena. There he studied the natural philosophy of Schelling. He moved to Freiberg in 1800 and came under the sway of Werner. Back in Copenhagen, his lectures drew such disfavour that he left. He took a professorship at Halle in 1804. In the War of Liberation he served as a volunteer and was present at the capture of Paris.
britannica-1911-tajik:
Tajik, also called Parsiwan, names a subject people of Afghanistan in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The text presents them as the first Persian holders of the soil. They still speak their mother tongue under Pathan rule. Their stock is described as a mix of Arab and Persian roots. In the country they till the fields, and in towns they keep shops and do clerk work.

They are never nomadic, the entry stresses. Dress and manners bring them close to the Afghans. Men from north of Kabul proved good fighters in the Afghan war of 1879 to 1880. Their count in Afghanistan was put at 900000. The name at first meant Arabs, then their kin born in Persia.
britannica-1911-travnik:
Travnik is the capital of a department in Bosnia, and a gazetteer entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes the town. It stands on the Lašva, a left hand branch of the Bosna river. The town lies forty four miles by rail north west of Serajevo. Its count in 1895 came to about 6,000 people.

Travnik is built mainly round a steep mass of rock. An ancient citadel crowns that rock. Mosques, palaces, arcades, and a fine bazaar survive among its narrow lanes. Those buildings bear witness to its former prosperity. Good modern barracks and public buildings stand there as well. Roman remains nearby suggest the town stands near the site of a Roman colony. It was a stronghold of the Bogomili in the fifteenth century. Its great period began in 1686, the entry notes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beda-francisc:
Beda Franciscus Dudik was a Moravian historian born near Kremsier in 1815, who died as abbot and titular bishop at Raigern in 1890. After Brünn and Olmütz, he entered the Benedictines in 1836 and was ordained in 1840. He taught classics, then history, at Brünn's gymnasium until 1854. He became Vienna's Privatdozent in 1855, Moravia's historiographer in 1859, and an Academy member in 1865.

Research trips took him to Sweden, Rome, France, Belgium, Holland, and Russia, and he founded the Teutonic Order's historical library at Vienna. A prolific writer drawing on sources, he published histories of Raigern, Moravian sources, Waldstein, and the Teutonic Order's coins and treasures. His chief work, the twelve-volume general history of Moravia (1860-89), runs to 1350, with its Przemyslian volumes translated into Czech.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eznik:
Eznik was a fifth-century Armenian writer, born at Golp in Taikh, a Chorokh tributary valley in north Armenia. He studied under Isaac the catholicos and Mesrop. At their request he traveled first to Edessa, then to Constantinople, to master the sciences and to gather Syriac and Greek manuscripts. He came home to Armenia after the Council of Ephesus in 431.

He is probably the Eznik, Bishop of Bagrevand, who sat in the Synod of Artashat in 449. Besides work on the new Bible version, he wrote his great treatise Against the Sects between 441 and 449. It holds four books: against heathens, against Parseeism, against Greek philosophers, and against Marcionism. He argues from the Bible more than from reason. He shows keen mind and wide learning, at home in Persian as in Greek letters, in choice classical Armenian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-von-pau:
Franz von Paula Hladnik, born at Idria in Carniola on 29 March 1773 and died at Laibach on 25 November 1844. He was an Austrian botanist and schoolmaster who built Laibach's schools and its flora. Son of a mining official, he studied philosophy and theology and was ordained priest in 1796. But weak health barred parish work, so that year he became scriptor in the Laibach Lyceum library, soon giving it up for forty years of teaching in Laibach schools. By 1803 he directed the Normal School, and from 1807 to failing sight he served as prefect of the gymnasium, which he brought to flourishing condition, earning the Emperor Francis's honourable distinction.

During the French occupation he became professor of botany and natural history in Laibach's Central School. He received land for a garden of Carniolan flora that soon held six hundred kinds of local plants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kaiserchronik:
The Kaiserchronik is a twelfth-century German epic poem, at once a legend of all the saints and a tangled history of emperors. It runs from Roman emperors through German kings and emperors to King Conrad III's crusade in 1147. Written about 1150, probably by an ecclesiastic of Ratisbon who backed the Guelphs, it is often ascribed to Konrad der Pfaffe, author of the Song of Roland. Its sources included the Chronicle of Ekkehard and the Annolied.

Twelve complete manuscripts and seventeen partial ones survive, proof of wide popularity, and the poem was continued twice in the thirteenth century. The original ended at verse 17,283; a Bavarian addition ran to 800 verses, and a Swabian one carried the story to the Interregnum of 1254 to 1273. Massmann published it in full between 1849 and 1854, but the best edition is Schröder's of 1892. Its language is fair and at times genuinely poetic.
